originalTitle: Ford promises not to sell your driving habits to data brokers
summary: Ford vowed to never sell customer driving data to third-party data brokers as part of a new privacy promise aimed at setting the automaker apart from competitors that have faced legal and regulatory blowback for sharing telematics with data brokers without authorization. content: Ford vowed to never sell customer driving data to third-party data brokers as part of a new privacy promise aimed at setting the automaker apart from competitors that have faced legal and regulatory blowback for sharing telematics with data brokers without authorization. As part of its new promise, Ford says it will strive to protect customer data by using aggregating and anonymizing techniques. It will also “provide clear and easy-to-understand information about how we use your personal information.” And while Ford says it will still use data to improve safety, it will allow customers to adjust how much or how little data they would prefer to share. In making an explicit pledge not to sell customer data to outside firms, Ford is trying to position itself as one of the better actors in an industry rife with shady practices. “We know that trust is earned,” Kristin Jones, chief privacy officer at Ford, writes in a blog post. “Protecting your personal information is one way we intend to earn it every day.” "“We know that trust is earned.”" - Kristin Jones, Ford’s chief privacy officer The promise comes in the wake of General Motors agreeing to pay $220 million to settle claims that it illegally sold driver and location information to data brokers. The agreement requires GM to limit the driving data it collects and obtain “express consent” from drivers before collecting their information. Other automakers have been caught with their hands in the customer data cookie jar. A recent examination of 21 vehicle brands found that every single one transmitted data to at least one third-party domain over Wi-Fi. Over half contacted domains that specialize in advertising, tracking, or analytics (ATA), like Adobe, LexisNexis, and Amplitude, which gather details about your vehicle or driving behavior to sell to insurance companies or target you with ads. In a recent report, Mozilla crowned modern connected cars “the worst category of products for privacy” ever reviewed. The global nonprofit found that 92 percent of the reviewed automakers provide drivers with little (if any) control over their personal data, with 84 percent sharing user data with outside parties. Ford said it surveyed over 1,000 US customers, both Ford and non-Ford owners, who agreed that privacy is a top concern while over half of the respondents said they understand that some data sharing is okay. Forty-one percent said they were extremely or very concerned about data privacy in the auto industry, which was less than other groups like social media companies, the government, and financial institutions. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/PrivacyPromise_1080x1350_01_17.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/PrivacyPromise_1080x1350_02_22.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/PrivacyPromise_1080x1350_03_20.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/PrivacyPromise_1080x1350_04_18.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] To be sure, Ford’s promise isn’t just words on a screen. In the US, the Federal Trade Commission stops companies from misleading the public through deceptive claims. If Ford publicly promises something like, “We never sell your driving data to brokers” but breaks that promise, the FTC and state attorneys general can step in. They can sue Ford, force the company to sign legally binding agreements to correct the issue, and impose substantial financial fines. It should be noted that a company’s blog post or public promise is not a legal contract. The actual rules that apply to you are found in Ford’s official privacy policy and connected vehicle terms. Those legal agreements contain standard exceptions that allow Ford to share your data, such as complying with police requests or working with outside service providers. Also, opting out of data sharing does come with tradeoffs. While Ford states that data collection depends on the features you want to use, turning off vehicle tracking or location sharing often disables key features like built-in navigation, remote start, and wireless software updates.

chineseContent: 福特发誓永远不会将客户驾驶数据出售给第三方数据经纪人，作为新隐私承诺的一部分，该承诺旨在使该汽车制造商与因未经授权与数据经纪人共享远程信息处理而面临法律和监管打击的竞争对手区分开来。作为新承诺的一部分，福特表示将努力通过使用聚合和匿名技术来保护客户数据。它还将“提供有关我们如何使用您的个人信息的清晰且易于理解的信息。”尽管福特表示仍将使用数据来提高安全性，但它将允许客户调整他们愿意共享的数据量。通过明确承诺不向外部公司出售客户数据，福特试图将自己定位为这个充斥着不正当行为的行业中更好的参与者之一。 “我们知道信任是赢得的，”福特首席隐私官克里斯汀·琼斯在一篇博客文章中写道。 “保护您的个人信息是我们每天赚取信息的一种方式。” “我们知道信任是赢得的。”——福特首席隐私官克里斯汀·琼斯 (Kristin Jones) 在做出这一承诺之前，通用汽车同意支付 2.2 亿美元，以了结其向数据经纪人非法出售驾驶员和位置信息的指控。该协议要求通用汽车限制其收集的驾驶数据，并在收集信息之前获得驾驶员的“明确同意”。其他汽车制造商也曾把手伸进客户数据饼干罐里。最近对 21 个汽车品牌的一项检查发现，每个品牌都通过 Wi-Fi 将数据传输到至少一个第三方域。超过一半的联系领域专门从事广告、跟踪或分析 (ATA)，例如 Adob​​e、LexisNexis 和 Amplitude，它们收集有关您的车辆或驾驶的详细信息
whyItMatters: 这条信息属于 AI 与科技趋势信号，适合用于观察工具选型、产品机会、开发者关注点和技术路线变化。
